notes: Ruling slot 4 = PPSh under Hoxha. Slot 7 = Sigurimi (Hazbiu/Shehu), 22 = People's Army under Balluku (MD armed-forces sprite), 13 = State Planning Commission (Këllezi, chairman 1968-75), 19 = Sino-Albanian Friendship Association as the pro-Beijing wing, 5 = Labour Youth Union as cultural-revolution radicals, 6 = the purged pro-Soviet Belishova-Tashko group. Émigrés follow MD: Legaliteti 0 (sprite), Balli Kombëtar 20 (PBK sprite), House of Zogu 23 (sprite); the Free Albania National Committee (active 1970, chaired by Rexhep Krasniqi) takes the Western-conservative slot 1 with popularity. Third League of Prizren (Xhafer Deva) as the fascist slot. Bektashi HQ (Tirana, closed 1967) in 8, the Michigan tekke in 9.

0.name: Lëvizja e Legalitetit
0.text:
The Legality Movement was founded in November 1943 by Abaz Kupi to restore King Zog's lawful rule and to fight both the occupiers and the communist partisans. Defeated in 1944, its fighters escaped abroad and took part in the failed Western-backed infiltrations of the early 1950s. Kupi, now in the United States, still leads it among the émigré communities of America, Italy and Turkey.

Legaliteti stands for the restoration of the Zogu monarchy as a strong, authoritarian but Western-aligned order, the protection of property and religion, and the liberation of Albania from communism with American and British help. It draws on the loyalty of Mati, Zog's homeland, and of the central highlands, and on a disciplined core of veterans who never accepted the abolition of the monarchy in 1946.

1.name: Komiteti Kombëtar Shqipëria e Lirë
1.text:
The Free Albania National Committee was constituted in Paris in 1949 with American and British backing to unite the anti-communist emigration: former members of Balli Kombëtar and the Legality Movement, the agrarian leagues and independents. Its men took part in the ill-fated Western infiltrations of the early 1950s. Since 1956 it has been chaired from New York by the historian Rexhep Krasniqi, while Abaz Ermenji heads its Paris branch.

The Committee speaks for a democratic, Western-oriented Albania with free elections, private property, religious freedom and protection for the Albanians of Yugoslavia. It lobbies Western governments and publishes the monthly Shqiptari i lirë. Its base is the emigration in the United States, Italy and Turkey; its weakness is the old feuds between its member groups and fading Western interest.

2.name: Vatra
2.text:
Vatra, the Pan-Albanian Federation of America, was founded in Boston in 1912 by Fan Noli and Faik Konica and became the voice of the Albanian emigrants of the New World. Noli's short-lived democratic government of 1924 grew out of its circles. Since Noli's death in 1965 the federation and its newspaper Dielli remain the oldest and largest Albanian organization in the United States.

Vatra stands for an independent, democratic and secular Albania governed by the rule of law, civil liberties and elected institutions, and for the national rights of the Albanians of Kosovo and Macedonia. It keeps its distance from the monarchists as well as from the Hoxha regime and looks to American democracy as its model. Its leverage lies in the money, votes and contacts of the Albanian-American community.

3.name: Reformistët e Tiranës
3.text:
The Tirana Reformers are a loose network of party intellectuals, editors and cultural officials in the capital, among them Fadil Paçrami and Todi Lubonja, veterans of the party press and youth apparatus who now hold senior posts in cultural life. They have no platform of their own, but they quietly encourage younger writers, composers and singers looking for air beyond the rigid canon of socialist realism.

They seek a socialism with fewer dogmas: lighter censorship, room for modern music and literature, more contact with Western Europe and more consumer goods for a long-suffering population. They never challenge Hoxha openly. Their following lies among students, young professionals and the urban intelligentsia of Tirana, and their danger is that the leadership treats any thaw as the first step toward revisionism.

4.name: Partia e Punës e Shqipërisë
4.text:
The Party of Labour of Albania has ruled since 1944, when the Communist Party founded in 1941 took power at the head of the partisan movement; it adopted its present name in 1948. Its First Secretary is Enver Hoxha, flanked by Prime Minister Mehmet Shehu and Hysni Kapo, and its leadership has survived by purging pro-Yugoslav and then pro-Soviet rivals in turn.

The party enforces the most rigid Stalinist order in Europe: full collectivization, central planning, a cult of self-reliance and, since 1967, the closure of every mosque and church. It denounces both American imperialism and Soviet revisionism, left the Warsaw Pact in 1968 and relies on China for aid. Its power rests on the party apparatus, the Sigurimi and the loyalty of the partisan generation.

5.name: Bashkimi i Rinisë së Punës së Shqipërisë
5.english: Union of Labour Youth of Albania
5.native_full: Bashkimi i Rinisë së Punës së Shqipërisë
5.text:
The Union of Labour Youth of Albania is the party's mass youth organization and the shock force of the Cultural and Ideological Revolution proclaimed in 1966. Its activists led the 1967 campaign against religion that began among students in Durrës, cover walls with 'lightning sheets' denouncing bureaucrats and backward customs, and fill the volunteer brigades building railways, terraces and drainage works.

Its most militant members want to push the revolution further: an end to officials' privileges, the rotation of cadres into manual work, the emancipation of women from clan custom and the uprooting of every trace of the old society. They admire China's Red Guards and distrust comfortable functionaries. Their leverage is numbers and enthusiasm among the young, whom the party needs and fears in equal measure.

6.name: Grupi Belishova–Tashko
6.text:
The Belishova–Tashko Group is the regime's name for the communists who sided with Moscow in the Soviet-Albanian split of 1960–61. Liri Belishova, a Politburo member and Central Committee secretary, and Koço Tashko, chairman of the party's Auditing Commission, were expelled for defending Khrushchev's line, while Rear Admiral Teme Sejko and others were executed in 1961. Both Belishova and Tashko now live in internment.

The pro-Soviet communists want Albania back in the socialist camp: reconciliation with Moscow and the Warsaw Pact, Soviet aid and a less isolated, more conventional communist state. They regard the alliance with distant China as a dangerous adventure. Their sympathisers among officers and specialists trained in the Soviet Union are silent and watched, and their leverage depends entirely on a change at the top.

7.name: Drejtoria e Sigurimit të Shtetit
7.text:
The Sigurimi, the Directorate of State Security, is Albania's political police, founded in 1944 and controlled since 1954 by Interior Minister Kadri Hazbiu, a close ally of Prime Minister Mehmet Shehu. With informers in every workplace and village, its prisons at Burrel and Spaç and its internment camps, it has made Albania one of the most thoroughly policed societies in the world.

The Sigurimi stands for permanent vigilance against the class enemy, the émigrés, Yugoslav and Soviet agents and any deviation within the party itself. It favours total isolation from the outside world and the punishment of whole families for the crimes of one member. Its leverage is immense: its files can end any career, and its loyalty to Shehu makes it a power bloc in its own right.

8.name: Kryegjyshata Botërore Bektashiane
8.text:
The Bektashi World Headquarters moved to Tirana in 1930 after Atatürk banned the Sufi orders in Turkey, making Albania the centre of the Bektashi Order, a Sufi brotherhood with Shia leanings that reveres Ali and the Twelve Imams. Its head, the dedebaba Ahmet Myftar Dede, saw the headquarters and every tekke closed in 1967, when Hoxha proclaimed Albania the world's first atheist state.

The Bektashis have long been the most liberal and patriotic of Albania's faiths, proud of their part in the national awakening, open to the equality of women and indifferent to outward ritual. They ask only for freedom of worship and the return of their tekkes. Their following is strongest in the south, around Gjirokastër, Korçë and Skrapar, where dervish devotion survives quietly in private homes.

9.name: Teqeja e Parë Shqiptare Bektashiane në Amerikë
9.english: First Albanian Bektashi Tekke in America
9.native_full: Teqeja e Parë Shqiptare Bektashiane në Amerikë
9.text:
The First Albanian Bektashi Tekke in America was founded in 1954 near Detroit by Baba Rexheb, a learned dervish who fled southern Albania in 1944. With the tekkes at home closed and their clergy dispersed, it has become the refuge of the order's teaching and the place where Albanian-American Bektashis gather for the mourning of Imam Husayn in Muharrem and the order's other feasts.

Baba Rexheb insists on preserving the order's doctrine and spiritual hierarchy intact, rejects any compromise with Hoxha's atheism and hopes to rebuild the authority of the babas in a liberated Albania. He is an uncompromising enemy of communism. His influence rests on his scholarship and on the loyalty of emigrant families from the south, who regard the tekke as the true seat of their faith.

10.name: Komuniteti Mysliman i Shqipërisë
10.text:
The Muslim Community of Albania was the official body of the country's Sunni majority, organized after the 1923 congress at which Albanian Muslims broke with the religious authority of Istanbul. Under communism it survived as a tightly controlled body until 1967, when its mosques were closed or demolished, its property seized and its clergy forced into secular work; scholars such as Hafiz Sabri Koçi were sent to prison.

Its surviving imams preach no politics, only the right of believers to pray, bury their dead according to Islam and teach the Qur'an to their children. They accepted state authority before and would again in exchange for tolerance. Their influence is invisible but deep, in families across central Albania who still keep the fast and pray in secret.

11.name: Muhaxhirët
11.text:
The Muhaxhirët are a pan-Islamist milieu among the Albanian Muslim families who settled in Turkey, Syria and Egypt after the Balkan Wars and the communist takeover, and among their children educated in Istanbul, Damascus and Cairo. Since 1967, when Tirana closed every mosque, a few of them have found in Hizb ut-Tahrir and similar movements an answer to the destruction of Islam in their homeland.

They teach that Albania's catastrophe proves the folly of nationalism and secular rule, and that only a restored caliphate uniting all Muslims can protect the faith. They despise the communist regime and the Western-backed émigré committees alike. No recognized figure leads them and their numbers are tiny, but they circulate pamphlets among Albanian emigrants and pilgrims to Mecca.

12.name: Albanian American Moslem Society
12.text:
The Albanian American Moslem Society, founded in Detroit in 1945, is the centre of Sunni Albanian life in exile. Its imam since 1949 is Vehbi Ismail, a graduate of al-Azhar from Shkodër, who in the early 1960s opened the Albanian Islamic Center in Harper Woods and has made it a hub of religious education, publishing and appeals on behalf of persecuted believers at home.

The Society calls for the restoration of religious freedom in Albania, a public role for Islam in a free society and the education of a new generation in the faith, combining piety with Albanian patriotism and anti-communism. It seeks ties with the wider Islamic world and Arab governments. Its leverage is modest: the dollars, letters and prayers of an emigrant community keeping Albanian Islam alive.

13.name: Komisioni i Planit të Shtetit
13.text:
The State Planning Commission drafts and supervises Albania's five-year plans and has been headed since 1968 by Abdyl Këllezi, a former finance minister and deputy prime minister. Around it and the economic ministries works a circle of planners and managers, among them the ministers Koço Theodhosi and Kiço Ngjela, responsible for industry and trade, the oil fields, the mines and the plants built with Chinese credits.

The technocrats want plans grounded in figures rather than slogans, more autonomy for enterprises, material incentives for workers and the freedom to buy Western machinery when Chinese aid falls short. They respect the party line but resent ideological campaigns in the economy. Their leverage lies in expertise and in the leadership's dependence on them to deliver growth.

14.name: Kisha Katolike në Shqipëri
14.text:
The Catholic Church in Albania, rooted among the northern Gegs of Shkodër, Mirdita and the highlands, was the country's intellectual seedbed before the war, with its Franciscan and Jesuit schools and writers such as Gjergj Fishta. Since 1945 the regime has executed or imprisoned most of its bishops and priests, and in 1967 it closed every church; Shkodër's cathedral is now a sports hall.

The Church stands for faith, family and the ancestral customs of the north, for freedom of worship and the rights of the Holy See, and is implacably anti-communist. It owes allegiance to Rome, but its strength is local: clan loyalties, mountain parishes and believers who still baptize their children in secret. Its surviving clergy, in prisons and labour camps, are martyrs to their people.

15.name: Bejlerët
15.text:
The Bejlerët are the great Muslim landowning families who dominated Albania under the Ottomans and King Zog: the Vlora, Toptani, Vrioni, Libohova and their peers, whose estates in the Myzeqe plain and the south once held thousands of sharecroppers. Expropriated by the land reform of 1945–46, they are scattered in exile in Italy, Turkey and the United States, while relatives left at home live in internment.

The beys want their land and property back, a conservative order in which the old families, merchants and clergy guide the nation, and close ties with Italy and the West. They despise the communists as upstarts but also distrust the populist nationalists of the emigration. Their leverage is wealth abroad, family networks and the prestige their names still carry among older Albanians.

16.name: Tregtarët e Korçës
16.text:
The Korçë Merchants are the former trading families of Korçë, Shkodër and Gjirokastër, Albania's most commercial and Western-minded towns, whose shops, workshops and import houses were nationalized after 1944. Many have relatives in America, Romania and Greece, and their sons, though barred from the best careers because of their class origin, remain the country's quiet reserve of business skill.

They want the right to trade, own shops and workshops, travel and receive money from abroad, under a modest state and an honest currency. Their models are the prewar bazaars and the Albanian emigrants who prospered in Boston and Bucharest. Without organization or recognized leader, their leverage lies in their skills, their connections abroad and the respect their families still command in the old towns.

17.name: Pylltarët
17.text:
The Foresters are the forestry engineers, botanists and hunting wardens of the state forest service who persuaded the government to proclaim Albania's first national parks in 1966, among them Dajti above Tirana, Llogara on the southern coast and Lura and Thethi in the northern mountains. They work with the natural scientists of the State University of Tirana and the youth afforestation brigades.

They want the remaining forests protected from the axes of the cooperatives, the lagoons and wetlands spared from total drainage and wildlife from unrestricted hunting, arguing that self-reliance must not mean destroying the country's own resources. They avoid open politics. Their influence is technical and local, but they speak for mountain villages that see their pastures and woods disappearing.

18.name: Bashkimet Profesionale të Shqipërisë
18.text:
The Trade Unions of Albania are the official labour federation, organized in 1945 and grouping the workers of the oil fields, mines, factories and state farms. Like every mass organization they serve as a transmission belt of the party, but they also run the social insurance funds, rest homes and workplace committees that make up most of the welfare Albanian workers receive.

Their officials press for higher wages, better housing and safer working conditions, and for a workers' voice in the management of enterprises, always within the party line. They back the campaigns against bureaucracy while defending the growing industrial working class against the planners' demands. Their leverage lies in the numbers of a young proletariat in Elbasan, Qyteti Stalin, Patos and Bulqizë that the regime cannot afford to alienate.

19.name: Shoqata e Miqësisë Shqipëri–Kinë
19.text:
The Sino-Albanian Friendship Association is the organization that channels Albania's alliance with Mao's China, presided over by members of the party leadership. Around it gather the officials, engineers and officers who manage Chinese loans and projects such as the metallurgical combine planned for Elbasan, the students trained in Beijing and the propagandists who translate and spread Mao's writings.

This pro-Chinese wing wants the alliance with Beijing deepened into a true model: continuing revolution, the mass line, people's war and campaigns against bureaucracy on the Chinese pattern. It sees Mao as the leader of the world anti-revisionist movement. Its leverage is China's aid, on which Albania's economy depends, but Hoxha is wary of any faction whose first loyalty might lie in Beijing rather than Tirana.

20.name: Balli Kombëtar
20.text:
Balli Kombëtar, the National Front, was founded in 1942 by Midhat Frashëri as a nationalist and republican resistance movement. Its truce with the occupiers and its war with the communist partisans ended in defeat in 1944, and its leaders fled abroad. In exile its most prominent figure is Abaz Ermenji in Paris, and its veterans form the backbone of the Free Albania National Committee.

The Ballists want an independent, republican and ethnically complete Albania, including Kosovo and the Albanian lands of Yugoslavia and Greece, with a free economy and strong national institutions. They are fiercely anti-communist and anti-Slav, and they look to the United States for support. Their base is the emigration in America, Italy and Turkey and the memory of their fighters in the south and in Kosovo.

21.name: Lidhja e Tretë e Prizrenit
21.text:
The Third League of Prizren is an émigré organization founded in the United States in 1946 by nationalists from Kosovo and revived in New York with American support in 1962. Since 1966 it has been led by Xhafer Deva, interior minister of the German-occupied Albanian state in 1943–44, who now lives in California; it publishes the magazine Lidhja e Prizrenit.

The League's programme is a Greater Albania uniting Kosovo, western Macedonia, Çamëria and the Albanian lands of Montenegro with the motherland, by armed force if necessary. Its leaders' wartime collaboration with the Axis and their hatred of Serbs set them apart from the democratic émigrés. Its base lies among Kosovar emigrants in the United States, Turkey and Western Europe and among veterans of the occupation regime.

22.name: Ushtria Popullore
22.text:
The Albanian People's Army grew out of the partisan National Liberation Army of 1942–44 and is commanded through the Ministry of People's Defence, headed since 1953 by Beqir Balluku, a Politburo member and partisan veteran. Since the break with Moscow it has been rearmed with Chinese weapons, and since 1968 it has adopted the doctrine of people's war waged by the whole nation in arms.

The army sees itself as the shield of the revolution against invasion from the Yugoslav, Soviet or NATO side, and its commanders press for modern armaments, professional training and a defence budget the economy can barely bear. Political commissars keep it loyal to the party. Its leverage is the prestige of its partisan generals and the fear of invasion that dominates Albanian politics.

23.name: Dinastia Zogu
23.text:
The House of Zogu reigned over Albania from 1928, when Ahmet Zogu proclaimed himself King Zog I, until the Italian invasion of April 1939 drove him into exile. Zog died in France in 1961, and an assembly of loyal émigrés in Paris proclaimed his son king as Leka I. Born in 1939, Leka lives in Spain, prepares for a return and cultivates contacts in conservative Western and Arab circles.

The dynasty stands for an independent Albanian kingdom, a strong monarchy uniting Muslims and Christians, and the overthrow of communism with Western and friendly Arab help. It relies on the Legality Movement and the clans of Mati. Its leverage is legitimacy: for many Albanians at home and abroad, the crown remains the last symbol of a free nation.
